idiom_name: public struct/class with internal storage compiled for ABI stability
implementation_notes: Swift builds the firewall into the compiler: in library evolution mode the fields of a public struct may be added, removed or reordered without breaking already-compiled clients, because clients reach them through non-inlinable accessors instead of baked-in offsets, and such types are called resilient. The realization is therefore 'public type, internal storage' - no pointer and no wrapper - with @usableFromInline and @inlinable as the explicit opt-outs that promise a stable ABI for the pieces you do expose, while @frozen makes the opposite promise and re-exposes the layout for speed. Inside an app target without library evolution the compiler treats every type as frozen, so the same source becomes an ordinary inline struct and the protection disappears.
pitfalls: Resilience is a build setting, not a keyword: without library evolution mode the compiler assumes a frozen layout, bakes the stored properties into clients, and the same source crashes on an ABI mismatch after an upgrade.
Non-inlinable accessors cost a call and block cross-module optimization; the usual cure, @frozen or @inlinable, gives back precisely the layout exposure the resilience bought.

Storage referenced from inlinable code or from a frozen struct has to be ABI-public (@usableFromInline), which quietly re-pins the representation - a common way to lose the protection without noticing.

variants.name: Value type backed by a private reference body
variants.idiom_name: public struct holding a private final class instance as its body
variants.implementation_notes: The literal pointer-to-body shape in Swift is a value type whose only stored property is a reference to a private final class holding the state and helper logic - the representation the standard library uses for its own containers. The body can then change freely and copies are cheap, but because the reference is shared, copies alias unless the accessors implement copy-on-write with isKnownUniquelyReferenced, so this is a deliberate choice rather than a default. Prefer it when the body is large, when reference identity or lifetime observation matters, or when the type must participate in delegate/observer relationships; otherwise plain resilient storage gives value semantics for free.
pitfalls: Copies share the class instance: without isKnownUniquelyReferenced-based copy-on-write, mutating one copy mutates them all, so value semantics have to be implemented explicitly rather than inherited.
Each instance pays a heap allocation and reference counting, and the invisible body defeats synthesis of Codable and Equatable on the outer type, so those conformances must be written by hand.
A class-backed store is not Sendable by default; adding concurrency checking forces an actor or lock around the body, which changes the type's API and its copy semantics.
